strengths: Strong and consistent empirical results across 46 datasets (MMEB and MMEB-V2), multiple model families (Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA), and scales (2B-32B), with FreeRet-7B matching and FreeRet-32B exceeding supervised methods

Well-motivated and thoroughly ablated technical contributions: lexicalization pressure analysis with rigorous probing experiments (Fig. 2), controlled generation via thoughtful prompt design (Table 3b), and discovery of LLM framing effects with systematic validation (Table 3c, Fig. 4)
Novel insight into framing effects in LLMs for retrieval, showing 8.4% improvement from Yes/No to MCQ framing and demonstrating correlation between lexical bias and accuracy
Comprehensive and reproducible evaluation with detailed prompting strategies, promised code release, clear experimental setup, and honest limitations discussion

Significant practical value: eliminates costly fine-tuning, enables immediate deployment across any MLLM, supports arbitrary modality combinations, preserves generative capabilities for RAG applications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual techniques are incremental engineering insights—removing final MLP is a simple heuristic, prompt constraints are straightforward, and MCQ framing directly applies prior work on cognitive framing effects

Weak theoretical justification: Lemma 1 oversimplifies by restating known properties of language modeling loss; the connection to why h^Attn_L preserves semantics better than h^MLP_L is loose and underexplored; 7% semantic similarity drop (94% → 87% in Fig. 2b) is not dramatic

Post-hoc explanatory framing: lexicalization pressure concept introduced after discovering MLP removal helps rather than theoretically predicted; framing effect explanations (e.g., pragmatic connotations of Yes/No) are speculative without rigorous validation; specific prompting choices lack principled justification

Efficiency concerns inadequately addressed: Section A.5 acknowledges higher MLLM latency than CLIP but proposes only standard solutions (pre-filtering, reranking limits) without concrete timing comparisons; practical deployment benefits claimed but not empirically validated

Experimental fairness issues: comparisons mix methods with different training data amounts (GME 8M, MMRet 26.2M, VLM2Vec 0.7M); no error analysis or failure case discussion; limited evaluation beyond MMEB/MMEB-V2; single omni-modal example (Fig. 6) for claiming arbitrary modality support

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 36+ datasets with consistent improvements over heavily trained baselines; FreeRet-2B outperforms models trained on 8M+ pairs
Novel empirical insights about lexicalization pressure and LLM framing effects supported by well-designed probing experiments (Figures 2, 8); cross-lingual analysis strengthens claims
Addresses practical problem of deploying MLLMs for retrieval without fine-tuning; enables omni-modal retrieval and preserves generative capabilities
Extensive ablation studies (Table 3) and generalization analysis (Table 6) across model families and scales; clear presentation with useful visualizations
Systematic investigation of each component with clear motivation; error analysis provided showing concrete failure modes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (removing MLP, prompt engineering, MCQ formatting) are relatively straightforward; primary contribution is identifying where existing techniques help rather than proposing novel methods

Theoretical justification for lexicalization pressure is incomplete; Appendix C provides simplified argument but doesn't rigorously explain why loss of semantic structure helps retrieval specifically; reliance on empirical correlation rather than causal analysis

Framing effect analysis lacks depth: explanation via 'social and pragmatic connotations' is speculative; connection between context-free bias (Fig 4 right) and retrieval performance is correlational; testing only 4 label pairs is limited

Computational efficiency concerns inadequately addressed: FreeRet has 50x+ latency penalty vs CLIP (0.47s vs <10ms), but Section F dismisses this by proposing orthogonal strategies that weaken the core contribution; practical deployment scenarios not discussed

Prompt design choices appear ad-hoc without systematic sensitivity analysis; unclear how much improvement stems from better prompts vs architectural modifications; limited exploration of alternative constraint designs
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing CLIP fine-tuned on same data, limited comparison with other training-free MLLM methods beyond E5-V; E5-V comparison unfair since it lacks reranking
Reproducibility gaps: temperature/sampling parameters not specified; sensitivity to exact prompt wording untested; how different MLLM architectures' layer structures affect the approach unclear
